blocks.text: Adaptive functioning is assessed with a standardised scale such as the Vineland Adaptive Behaviour Scale, and information should be gathered from one or more independent sources.

Mild **LD**: speech delay but usable communication skills, academic ceiling up to ~6th-grade level, generally independent self-care, may hold paid employment. Moderate **LD**: deficits in language use/comprehension, academic ceiling 2nd-3rd grade, unskilled/semiskilled work with support, majority have an identifiable organic aetiology. Severe **LD**: poor motor development, minimal verbal speech, partial self-maintenance only under close supervision. Profound **LD**: very limited comprehension/language, needs assistance with most ADLs and nursing-level care, clear organic aetiology in most cases, frequent comorbid neurological/physical disability (including epilepsy, visual and hearing impairment).

blocks.text: **LD** prevalence is estimated at 1-==3%== of the population; incidence is hard to establish because milder cases may go unrecognised until middle childhood. Highest incidence is in school-age children, peaking at ages 10-14; **LD** is ~1.5x more common in males than females.
Severity distribution of **LD**: Mild ==85%==, Moderate ==10%==, Severe ==4%==, Profound 1-==2%==.

Up to two-thirds of children and adults with **LD** have comorbid mental health problems; psychopathology risk rises with **LD** severity. Disruptive/conduct-disorder behaviours are more common in **MILD** **LD**, whereas severe **LD** carries a particularly high rate of autism spectrum disorder/pervasive developmental disorder.
Comorbid seizure disorders occur in ~==16%== overall (up to ==50%== in profound **LD**); hearing loss is seen in 25-==42%== of community samples of people with **LD**.

**CIPOLD** (Confidential Inquiry into Premature Deaths of People with Learning Disabilities): men and women with **LD** die on average 13 and 20 years earlier respectively than the general population, reflecting poorer general health and barriers to timely, appropriate healthcare.
Aetiological timing of **LD**: ~50-==70%== attributable to a prenatal factor (defects in embryogenesis), 10-==20%== to a perinatal factor, and 5-==10%== to a postnatal factor.

blocks.text: Genetic causes: autosomal chromosome disorders (e.g. Down's syndrome), sex chromosome disorders, deletions/duplications, autosomal dominant/recessive disorders, X-linked recessive/dominant conditions, presumed polygenic conditions (neural tube defects, pervasive developmental disorders), and mitochondrial/metabolic disorders.

External prenatal factors: infections (rubella, cytomegalovirus, syphilis, toxoplasmosis, **HSV**, **HIV**); exposure to medication, alcohol, opioids, or toxins such as lead; maternal illness (diabetes, hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism, hypertension, malnutrition).

Perinatal factors: prematurity/low birth weight; infections (meningitis, encephalitis, neonatal septicaemia, pneumonia); problems around delivery (birth asphyxia, intracranial haemorrhage, birth injury); newborn complications (respiratory distress, hyperbilirubinaemia, hypoglycaemia).

Postnatal factors (first years of life): **CNS** infection, intracranial tumour, hypoxic brain injury, head injury (RTAs, household accidents, child abuse), toxic agent exposure, and adverse psychosocial environment (family instability, frequent moves, inadequate caretaking).
Head injury is a classic example of a postnatal (not perinatal or genetic) risk factor for **LD**, distinct from birth asphyxia (perinatal) or neonatal septicaemia (perinatal).

Later epidemiological studies have not supported this division, and the psychosocial-causation idea behind 'subcultural' **LD** remains controversial.

blocks.text: Normalisation was first developed in 1960s Scandinavia (Bengt Nirje) and extended by Wolf Wolfensberger (1972), who argued institutions 'dehumanised' residents. Wolfensberger's concept of 'social role valorisation' (**SRV**) proposes that poor attitudes to people with **LD** can be countered by creating opportunities for valued social roles (family member, neighbour, employee); **SRV** further incorporates respect, opportunity, competence-building, independent living and individual choice.

Valuing People (2001) is the **UK** government White Paper defining **LD** for health/social care purposes; the same policy framework later set out four key principles — rights, independence, choice, and inclusion — for people with **LD**. Deinstitutionalisation (from the 1980s) shifted care from institutions towards the community, complicated by community attitudes toward people with **LD**.

Community mental health/**LD** multidisciplinary teams typically include occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, physiotherapy, psychology and psychiatry, working alongside general adult psychiatry and primary care.

Estimated **LD** prevalence among **UK** offenders is 1-==10%== (up to ==30%== have a learning difficulty); Prison Reform Trust data: ==7%== of prisoners have an **IQ** below 70 and ==25%== have an **IQ** below 80. Most offences are committed by those with borderline/mild **LD**, not severe **LD**.

Lord Bradley's report (2009) reviewed people with mental health problems or **LD** in the criminal justice system and called for more information at all stages (arrest, sentencing, diversion, treatment, reoffending reduction). Criminal justice liaison and diversion teams link criminal justice agencies with health/social care services.
Offending in the **LD** population is committed predominantly by those with borderline and mild **LD** rather than severe **LD**.

sections.title: 6. Psychiatric Comorbidity — Epidemiology, Diagnostic Difficulties & Assessment Tools

blocks.text: Total prevalence of mental health problems in adults with **LD** lies between 30-==50%==, higher in more severe **LD**. Deb et al (2001a): a statistically significant association between rate of psychiatric illness and increasing age in people with **LD**.

Hastings et al (2004): ==46.3%== of adults with **LD** experienced ≥1 life event in the preceding year (similar to the general population), yet psychiatric illness prevalence was much higher (==32.2%== vs ==11.2%== in the general population). Physical illness was also higher (only ==6%== reported no illness vs ==37%== of the general population); epilepsy prevalence ==22.1%==; poor eyesight in ==19%== (vs ==8%== general population); ==28.8%== overweight, ==23.6%== obese.

blocks.text: Diagnostic overshadowing: once a major diagnosis is made, other coexisting problems tend to be wrongly attributed to it. Symptoms of physical ill health are commonly mistakenly attributed to a mental-health/behavioural problem or considered 'inherent' to the person's **LD** (Emerson & Baines 2010). Current psychiatric classification systems were developed on populations that excluded people with **LD**, and deficits in language/abstract thinking make emotional symptoms harder to identify.

blocks.text: Schizophrenia is ~3-fold more common in **LD** than the general population (prevalence ~3-==3.5%==); mean age of onset is earlier (~23 years). In severe **LD**, thought disorder and complex persecutory delusions are **LESS** evident; unexplained aggression, bizarre behaviour, labile mood and increased mannerisms/stereotypies dominate instead. Diagnosis is difficult but symptoms often respond to a neuroleptic trial. Self-talk is a normal developmental phenomenon (not psychosis) particularly common in children with Down's syndrome and in autism.

A stem asks for the **FALSE** statement about schizophrenia in **LD**; the trap answer is 'thought disorder is probably more evident' — in reality thought disorder and complex persecutory delusions are **LESS** evident in severe **LD**, where unexplained aggression/bizarre behaviour dominate instead.

blocks.text: Bipolar affective disorder prevalence is 2-==12%== (higher than general population). Unlike schizophrenia, the diagnosis can still be made in severe **LD** using biological features of mania/depression. Mood elevation in mania is often not verbalised — look for hyperactivity, wandering, mutism, and unexplained challenging behaviour as symptom equivalents.

Depression prevalence ~2-==4%==; depressed mood is often not vocalised, particularly in more severe **LD**, but may be observable. Biological features (diurnal variation) tend to be more marked. Irritability is a key symptom in young people with **LD**. Behavioural markers: self-absorption, pica, rocking, psychomotor retardation, tearfulness, refusal to eat, sleep disturbance. Suicide is very rare in severe **LD**; suicidal thoughts/acts occur more often in borderline-moderate **LD**.

Anxiety disorders are at least as common — probably more common — in **LD** than the general population; most common are simple phobia, social phobia, and **GAD**. **OCD** prevalence ==2.5%== (higher than general population), with ordering the most common compulsion. Genetic associations: Fragile X syndrome → social anxiety disorder; Prader-Willi and Rubinstein-Taybi syndromes → **OCD** (Levitas and Read 1998); Williams syndrome → anxiety disorder and phobias (Einfield et al 2001); Cornelia de Lange syndrome → compulsive behaviour (Hyman et al 2001).

blocks.text: Around 75-==80%== of children with autism also have **LD**; autism spectrum disorder is present in ~==10%== of people with mild **LD** and ~==40%== of those with severe **LD**. Associated medical conditions include epilepsy, tuberous sclerosis, congenital rubella syndrome, and phenylketonuria. Comorbid problems in autism+**LD** include **ADHD**, **OCD**, anxiety, depression, and tics; aggressive/auto-aggressive/disruptive behaviours should be treated as secondary disorders, not attributed to the autism itself.

Autism heritability is approximately 80-==90%== — one of the most heritable common medical conditions. Sibling recurrence risk is <==10%== if only one child in the family is affected so far, rising to ~==35%== if ≥2 children are already affected.

It is not a diagnosis itself — often it communicates frustration, anxiety, or stress.

blocks.text: Predisposing factors for behavioural problems in **LD**: sensory disability, poor communication, epilepsy, physical illness (ear infection, dental problems, constipation), medication, limited coping strategies, abuse, and environmental factors.

Challenging behaviour occurs in ~==7%== of all people with **LD**, rising to ==14%== in hospital settings; more common in severe **LD**, in men, and in the 15-34 age range. Broader behaviour disorders (aggression, self-injury, property destruction, restlessness, shouting, disruptive/antisocial behaviour) occur in 20-==44%== of the **LD** population.

Self-injurious behaviour (**SIB**): 10-==50%== of people with **LD** display **SIB** at some point (Borthwick-Duffy, 1994); prevalence is setting-dependent — hospital 8-==15%==, special school 3-==12%==, day centre 3-==10%==, home 1-==4%==. More common with moderate-severe **LD** (**IQ**<50), most frequent between ages 10-30, peaking at 15-20. Genetic associations: Prader-Willi, fragile X, Tourette's, Smith-Magenis, Cornelia de Lange, Lesch-Nyhan syndromes (Gates, 2003) — treating an underlying cause (e.g. gastric reflux in Cornelia de Lange) can reduce **SIB**. Wiseley et al (2002): endogenous-opioid hypothesis of **SIB** (analgesic or euphoric effect); opiate blockers **naloxone**/**naltrexone** can reduce **SIB**. Common forms: head-banging, biting, scratching, hair-pulling, pica.

Pica (persistent eating of non-nutritive items): occurs in ~==30%== of children aged 1-4; adult **LD** prevalence 10-==20%== in hospital/care units vs ~==5%== in the community. Associated with male sex (M:F 1.4:1), poor cognitive functioning, autism, and non-verbal status; good ADLs is protective. More common in severe **LD** and autism spectrum disorder, and less common with advancing age; managed with behavioural principles (McAdam et al, 2004). Autism spectrum disorder is the option most strongly associated with pica among people with **LD**.
Self-injurious behaviour is most frequent between the ages of 5 and 20 years.

blocks.text: In adults with **LD**, the most commonly reported **PTSD** symptoms remain nightmares, jumpiness and trouble sleeping (Helzer et al, 1987), but an exaggerated startle response is often seen. In half of those affected, symptoms lasted <6 months; in a third, symptoms persisted >1 year. **PTSD** rarely occurs in isolation — comorbidity with other psychiatric disorders is the norm. Diagnosis is hindered by communication difficulties in severe **LD**, so behaviour/functional change (aggression, regression, altered sleep) may be the main clue, and symptoms risk being misattributed to other diagnoses.

blocks.text: General prescribing principle: treatment should be diagnosis-driven. People with **LD** are more susceptible to **CNS** side effects ('start low, go slow') and more likely to have comorbid physical health problems, so drug interactions require particular care.

blocks.note: The source material states general principles ('start low, go slow'; drug classes used for specific target symptoms) but gives no specific starting doses, titration schedules, or plasma-level targets for the **LD** population. Verify against the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry (15th ed.) chapter on prescribing in intellectual disability before relying on any numeric dose in practice or in an exam answer.

blocks.subtopic: STOMP and current UK policy on psychotropics for behaviour that challenges
blocks.note: The source notes describe antipsychotic use for behavioural disturbance and stereotypies but do not mention the **NHS** England **STOMP** (Stopping Over-Medication of People with a learning disability) initiative or current **NICE** guidance (**NG11**, 'Challenging behaviour and learning disabilities: prevention and interventions') on minimising and reviewing psychotropic prescribing for challenging behaviour. This is high-yield, contemporary exam content — verify against current **NICE** guidance.

blocks.text: Antipsychotics treat comorbid psychosis (e.g. schizophrenia) and acute behavioural disturbance; low doses also reduce stereotypies. Both oral and depot agents are used. Second-generation drugs such as **risperidone** are tried first for psychotic symptoms in an inpatient/ward scenario.
Antidepressants (SSRIs such as **citalopram** tried first) help depression, **OCD**, self-injurious behaviour, and other anxiety disorders.

Anticonvulsants such as **carbamazepine** treat episodic dyscontrol and improve underlying epilepsy control; rapid-cycling mood disorder and mixed affective states (more common in **LD**) may respond better to **carbamazepine** or **valproate** than to other agents.

**Lithium** is useful for bipolar disorder and antidepressant augmentation, and also reduces aggressive outbursts; it is licensed for the 'control of aggressive behaviour or intentional self-harm'. Baseline **EEG** plus renal function and cell counts are required before starting, because even therapeutic **lithium** doses may induce seizures in those with epilepsy, and pre-existing **EEG** changes increase susceptibility to **lithium** toxicity (Frith Prescribing Guidelines, p.99).
**Lithium** is licensed for the treatment of self-injurious behaviour and aggression in people with intellectual disability.

blocks.text: Stimulants (e.g. **methylphenidate**) are used for comorbid **ADHD**. Opiate antagonists (e.g. **naltrexone**) may decrease repetitive self-injurious behaviour acutely but are less effective long-term. Anti-libidinal drugs (cyproterone acetate, medroxyprogesterone acetate — which reduce testosterone) are indicated for severely problematic sexualised behaviour/sexual offending. Beta-blockers (e.g. **propranolol**) may reduce peripheral manifestations of anxiety.

blocks.text: A **UK** survey of clinical psychologists (Nagel and Leiper) found ==80%== used behavioural interventions, ==35%== used **CBT** techniques, and ==17%== used psychodynamic methods for people with **LD**.

**CBT** evidence in the **LD** population comes largely from forensic secure settings, effective for anxiety, depression, anger management, and sex offending (Sturmey, 2004); cognitive approaches can be adapted for borderline, mild, or moderate **LD**.

Behavioural treatments (operant-conditioning techniques such as shaping and chaining) teach basic skills (feeding, toileting) and establish normal behaviour patterns; they also help teach complex skills (relaxation, social skills) and can change maladaptive behaviours (phobias, inappropriate sexual behaviour). Behaviour analysts use antecedent-behaviour-consequence (**ABC**) charts to manage challenging behaviour. Family therapy (available in some services) targets the person with **LD** and their support network.

blocks.text: Down's syndrome is the most common genetic cause of **LD**; overall incidence ~1/1,000 live births. The major risk factor is maternal age >40; a previous translocation-type Down's child raises the recurrence risk further.

blocks.text: Clinical features: hypotonia, oblique palpebral fissures, flat nasal bridge, brachycephaly, high-arched palate, protruding tongue, atlanto-axial instability, Brushfield spots, epicanthic folds, low-set ears. Hands show short broad hands with a single palmar (simian) crease, syndactyly, clinodactyly, and altered dermatoglyphics. Congenital heart defects occur in ~==50%== (**VSD**, mitral valve disease, **PDA**); **GI** (oesophageal atresia, Hirschsprung disease), eye (strabismus, myopia), ear (otitis media, sensorineural deafness) and endocrine (hypothyroidism, diabetes) abnormalities also occur.
All of short/broad hands with a single palmar crease, syndactyly (webbed fingers), clinodactyly (incurved fingers), and altered dermatoglyphics are seen in the hands of people with Down's syndrome.

blocks.text: Fragile X syndrome: incidence ~1/3,000; the most common **INHERITED** cause of **LD**, accounting for 10-==12%== of **LD** in men. Caused by a **CGG** trinucleotide-repeat expansion at Xq27.3 (**FMR1** gene), giving the chromosome its 'fragile' appearance; X-**LINKED** **DOMINANT** inheritance with low penetrance, greater in males than females (due to the protective second normal X chromosome in females). Nearly ==50%== of affected children meet criteria for autism.

A 'which is **NOT** correct' Fragile X stem includes the distractor that **CGG** repeats occur on a fragile site of the Y chromosome — the repeat is actually on the X chromosome (Xq27.3, **FMR1** gene). Confusing X with Y exploits the syndrome's X-linked inheritance.

blocks.text: Fragile X syndrome is both the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and the mode of inheritance is X-linked dominant.

blocks.text: Fragile X clinical features: large head, large ears, long narrow face, short stature, post-pubertal macro-orchidism, hyperextensible joints. Epileptic seizures in 20-==25%==. Mild **LD** is typical in affected women; moderate/severe **LD** in affected men. Behavioural: hyperactivity, inattention, anxiety (particularly social anxiety), stereotypies, speech/language delay (palilalia, echolalia, cluttering, over-detailed speech), shyness, gaze avoidance, poor peer relationships. Brain imaging: enlarged ventricles/hippocampus/caudate nuclei, reduced posterior cerebellar vermis.

A vignette of autistic traits, conversational rigidity, palilalia, anxiety and poor eye contact in a male points to Fragile X syndrome — the most common inherited cause of **LD** and the most common single-gene cause of autism.

blocks.text: Fragile X and **IQ**: the higher the **CGG**-repeat number, the **LOWER** the **IQ** (inverse relationship). The **IQ** drop in affected males is most pronounced between ages 8-12 and stabilises by puberty (~15y); adaptive skills then continue to improve — Fragile X is **NOT** a degenerative condition. There is also a relationship between the length of the trinucleotide repeat and level of intelligence, and the drop correlates with **FMR1** methylation status.

Fragile X **IQ** questions test that **CGG** repeat length is **INVERSELY** related to **IQ** and that the **IQ** drop stabilises by puberty (~15y) with continued improvement afterward — distractors implying ongoing 'cognitive degeneration' wrongly suggest a progressive/dementing course, which Fragile X is not.

blocks.text: Turner syndrome (45,X) is a sex chromosome **MONOSOMY**; incidence 1/2,000-1/5,000 female births; ==99%== of conceptions end in spontaneous abortion or stillbirth. Features: short stature, low hairline, low-set ears, broad chest, widely-spaced nipples, webbed neck, obesity; ovarian failure before birth so puberty does not occur naturally; hyperactivity/distractibility in childhood, poor social skills/low self-esteem in adolescence. Does **NOT** typically cause **LD** — intelligence and verbal ability are usually normal. ==12%== have a **VSD** or aortic coarctation.

Triple X syndrome (47,**XXX**): incidence ~1/1,000 female births; 60-==70%== have mild **LD**; delayed language development, motor coordination problems, accelerated growth until puberty, premature ovarian failure; associated with anxiety and possibly increased schizophrenia incidence.

Klinefelter syndrome (47,**XXY**): incidence 1/500-1/1,000 male births; sterility is the primary feature; sparse body hair, hypogonadism, gynaecomastia; taller than average (~4cm), thin build, median **IQ** ~90 (skewed, most 60-70); introverted, less assertive/sociable, poorer school performance (reading/spelling). It is a sex-chromosome **TRISOMY**, not a deletion/duplication syndrome.

Klinefelter syndrome is characterised by hypogonadism, taller-than-average stature, median **IQ** ~90, and karyotype 47,**XXY** — but there is no established higher incidence in prison populations for Klinefelter syndrome specifically.

blocks.text: Prader-Willi syndrome: deletion or unexpressed genes on the **PATERNAL** chromosome 15 (q11-13); M:F 4:3; incidence 1/10,000-1/25,000. Early features: hypotonia, lethargy, hypogonadism, feeding/swallowing problems (triangular mouth), excessive sleepiness. Childhood: hyperphagia in ==80%==, insatiable appetite, food stealing. Adult features: obesity, hypotonia, infertility, hypogonadism, sparse pubic hair, extreme flexibility, prominent nasal bridge/forehead, small hands/feet, almond-shaped eyes, flattened face, thin upper lip, downturned mouth, striae. Behavioural phenotype: food obsession, skin-picking, impulsivity, aggression, **OCD**; autistic features in only ~==15%==; **IQ**<70 in >==90%==.
A microdeletion on the paternal 15q12 segment causes Prader-Willi syndrome.

Happy disposition, paroxysmal laughter, hand-flapping/clapping, ataxia, attraction to water; severe/profound **LD**; facial features (fair hair/blue eyes in ==66%==, microcephaly, flattened occiput, wide mouth, thin upper lip); epilepsy in over ==90%== with a characteristic **EEG** evident from age 3.
Angelman syndrome is characterised by severe/profound (not mild or moderate) intellectual disability, with ~==86%== of individuals affected by epilepsy.

blocks.text: Williams syndrome: deletion of ~26 genes on the long arm of chromosome 7; incidence 1/7,500-1/20,000. Elfin-like face; >==60%== have high serum calcium (managed with low-calcium diet/vitamin D restriction); mild-moderate **LD** (**IQ** 40-80, mean 56); short stature, broad forehead, hoarse voice, cardiovascular abnormalities (supravalvular aortic stenosis), thyroid abnormalities. Can be anxious/fearful with peer-relationship difficulty and hypersensitivity, **OR** conversely outgoing/disinhibited/excessively friendly; verbal skills better than motor/visuospatial skills.
Hypercalcaemia with supravalvular aortic stenosis and elfin facial features are characteristic of Williams syndrome.

blocks.text: Cri-du-chat syndrome: partial deletion at 5p15.2 (~==85%== de novo, majority paternal origin); incidence 1/15,000-1/50,000; more common in females (4:3). High-pitched cat-like cry in infancy; microcephaly, round face with hypertelorism, epicanthal folds, slanting palpebral fissures, broad flat nose, low-set ears, micrognathia, dental malocclusion; severe-profound **LD**; hyperactivity common (may improve with age), also stereotypies/self-injury/tantrums; respiratory/ear infections, congenital heart disease, **GI** abnormalities.
A child with a round face, hypertelorism, slanting palpebral fissures, broad flat nose, and an infantile cat-like cry has Cri-du-chat syndrome.

blocks.text: Smith-Magenis syndrome: complete/partial deletion of 17p11.2; incidence ~1/25,000; >==75%== mild/moderate **LD**. Flattened mid-face, abnormal upper lip, short hands/feet, single transverse palmar crease, high-arched palate, protruding tongue; severe self-injury (biting, hitting, head-banging), self-hugging stereotypy, sleep disturbance (reduced/absent **REM**), reduced pain/heat sensitivity; cognitive severity correlates with deletion size.

DiGeorge/velo-cardio-facial syndrome: microdeletion of chromosome 22 (22q11.2), ==90%== de novo, ==10%== inherited; prevalence estimated around 1/2,000-1/4,000. >==50%== mild/moderate **LD**; cardiac abnormalities (tetralogy of Fallot, **VSD**, interrupted aortic arch, pulmonary atresia); facial features (microcephaly, cleft palate, small mouth, long face, narrow palpebral fissure, minor ear abnormalities); hypocalcaemia in ==60%==; seizures; short stature; hearing/renal problems; hypospadias in ==10%== of males; long thin hands. Associated with schizophrenia-like psychosis and blunted/inappropriate affect.
Velo-cardio-facial (DiGeorge) syndrome occurs in around ==1 in 2==,000 people, is caused by a chromosome 22 (not 21) microdeletion, and is not usually associated with severe **LD** or dementia.

Moderate-severe **LD**; short stature, microcephaly, prominent nose, broad nasal bridge, hypertelorism, ptosis, broad thumbs/first toes; feeding difficulties, congenital heart disease, **EEG** abnormalities, seizures; friendly disposition, self-stimulatory behaviour, performance **IQ** > verbal **IQ**, intolerance of loud noise.

bullets.text: Angelman syndrome: maternal 15q12 deletion; happy disposition, paroxysmal laughter, hand-flapping, attraction to water; severe/profound LD; epilepsy in over ==90%==.
Williams syndrome (7q deletion, ~26 genes): elfin face, >==60%== hypercalcaemia, supravalvular aortic stenosis, mild-moderate LD (mean IQ 56), verbal skills > visuospatial.
Cri-du-chat (5p15.2 deletion): high-pitched cat-like cry, microcephaly, hypertelorism, severe-profound LD.
Smith-Magenis (17p11.2 deletion): severe self-injury with self-hugging stereotypy, reduced/absent REM sleep, reduced pain sensitivity.
DiGeorge/velo-cardio-facial (22q11.2 microdeletion, ==90%== de novo): cardiac defects, hypocalcaemia ==60%==, associated with schizophrenia-like psychosis.
Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome: moderate-severe LD, broad thumbs/first toes, friendly disposition, performance **IQ** > verbal **IQ**.
Prader-Willi childhood hyperphagia in ==80%== with insatiable appetite/food stealing; autistic features in only ~==15%==; **IQ**<70 in >==90%==.

blocks.text: Tuberous sclerosis complex (**TSC1**/**TSC2**): equal sex distribution; **LD** of all degrees; seizures in ==90%== of cases (infantile spasms/'salaam attacks' often the initial presentation); hamartomas of the **CNS**, depigmented ('ash leaf') skin patches, nail fibromas, cardiac/renal tumours. Autism, hyperactivity, impulsivity, aggression, self-injurious behaviour and sleep disturbance are all associated; **LD** spectrum ranges from absent (==30%==) to profound.
Tuberous sclerosis is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner (unlike Sanfilippo, Hunter, Hurler, or Lesch-Nyhan syndromes, which are recessive).

blocks.text: Neurofibromatosis type 1 (**NF1**): equal sex distribution; caused by a chromosome-17 mutation affecting cell division control, causing tumours along the **CNS**. **NIH** diagnostic criteria include: ≥6 café-au-lait spots (>5mm pre-pubertal, >15mm post-pubertal); ≥2 neurofibromas of any type or 1 plexiform neurofibroma; axillary/inguinal freckling; optic glioma; ≥2 Lisch nodules; a distinctive osseous lesion; or a first-degree relative with **NF1**. ~==50%== have speech/language difficulty; ==10%== have moderate-profound **LD** with verbal **IQ** > performance **IQ**; distractible, impulsive, hyperactive, anxious, possibly increased mood/anxiety disorder incidence.

A vignette with depigmented 'ash leaf' skin patches, seizures, and **CNS**/lung/kidney tumours points to tuberous sclerosis, not neurofibromatosis — café-au-lait spots (**NF1**) vs ash-leaf spots (tuberous sclerosis) are commonly swapped distractors in genetics EMIs.

blocks.text: Sturge-Weber syndrome: **LD**, epilepsy, and hemiparesis, associated with port-wine stains and angiomas of the meninges (temporal/occipital areas).

bullets.text: Tuberous sclerosis (**TSC1**/**TSC2**, autosomal dominant): seizures in ==90%== (often infantile spasms first), CNS hamartomas, ash-leaf skin patches; LD ranges from absent (==30%==) to profound.
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (chromosome 17): café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, Lisch nodules; ~==50%== speech/language difficulty, ==10%== moderate-profound LD with verbal IQ > performance IQ.
Ash-leaf spots (tuberous sclerosis) vs café-au-lait spots (**NF1**) — a commonly swapped EMI distractor pair.

blocks.text: Phenylketonuria (**PKU**): autosomal recessive deficiency of phenylalanine hydroxylase → phenylalanine build-up; preventable and all **UK** newborns are screened. Symptoms absent neonatally; untreated features include microcephaly, skin hypopigmentation, language delay, severe **LD**, hyperactivity, self-injury, and a 'musty/mouse-like' skin odour; seizures develop later (==25%== generalized). Managed by dietary/medical phenylalanine restriction — not curable.
An autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance occurs in phenylketonuria (not Hunter disease, Fragile X, tuberous sclerosis, or Lesch-Nyhan syndrome).

blocks.text: Hurler syndrome: alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency → glycosaminoglycan accumulation. Short stature, hepatosplenomegaly, coarse facial features (hirsutism, corneal clouding, large tongue). Developmental arrest by age 2-4, then progressive mental decline and loss of physical skills; associated hearing loss; death often before age 10.

Sanfilippo disease: disorder of heparan sulphate breakdown; incidence 1/70,000. Severe **LD**, claw hand, dwarfism, hypertrichosis, hearing loss, hepatosplenomegaly, biconvex lumbar vertebrae, joint stiffness; behavioural problems include restlessness, sleep problems, and challenging behaviour (a prominent sleep disorder is a distinguishing behavioural feature). Poor prognosis; death typically between ages 10 and 20, usually from respiratory tract infection.

Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome: multiple loci (11q13, 11q21, 15q22, 3p13). Retinitis pigmentosa, polydactyly (extra digits), spastic paraplegia, night blindness (red cone atrophy), hypogonadism, **NIDDM**, renal problems, central obesity; associated with mild-moderate **LD**.

Lesch-Nyhan syndrome: X-linked recessive defect on the long arm of the X chromosome causing **HGPRT** deficiency and consequent uric acid build-up (partial deficiency causes gout); virtually all affected individuals are male. Early hypotonia and delayed motor milestones; extrapyramidal signs (spasticity, choreoathetoid movements) from ~9 months; hyperreflexia/clonus by 1 year; seizures in ==50%==. Compulsive/uncontrollable self-injury (biting of lips/tongue/fingers) usually presents between ages 2-3, with physical/verbal aggression toward others emerging in adulthood; failure of secondary sexual development. Death is usually due to renal failure (infection or uric acid deposition).
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is characterised by compulsive self-mutilation, not hydrocephalus, hepatic failure, hypertonia, or normal secondary sexual characteristics.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Hunter syndrome: X-linked recessive deficiency of iduronate sulfatase → glycosaminoglycan accumulation; incidence 1/130,000 males. Coarse face, flat nasal bridge, flared nostrils, hearing loss, ataxia, hernia, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness, recurrent ear/respiratory infections, growth retardation, cardiovascular abnormalities. Hyperactivity, speech loss at 8-10y, restlessness, sleep abnormalities. Those **WITH** associated **LD** have shorter life expectancy (~15y) than those without (~20-30y); death is due to neurodegeneration/physical complications.

expansion: Lesch-Nyhan syndrome — **HGPRT** deficiency, uric acid build-up, X-linked recessive
Hunter syndrome — iduronate sulfatase deficiency, glycosaminoglycan build-up, X-linked recessive

blocks.text: Hunter syndrome is the X-linked recessive condition among the listed mucopolysaccharidoses (distinguished from the autosomal recessive Hurler and Sanfilippo diseases).

blocks.text: Hunter syndrome (X-linked recessive, iduronate sulfatase deficiency) is easily confused with the similarly-named Hurler syndrome (autosomal recessive, alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency) — the exam exploits the near-identical names and overlapping mucopolysaccharidosis features.

blocks.text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome: mostly spontaneous mutations; the **NIPBL** gene (chromosome 5) accounts for ~half of cases. Usually moderate/severe **LD**. Low birth weight, short stature, developmental delay, microcephaly, hypertrichosis, long philtrum, small upturned nose, downturned lips, low-set ears, and **SMALL** (not large) hands/feet. Behavioural problems: self-stimulation, aggression, self-injury, rigid routine preference, autism-like features; also **GI** reflux, congenital heart defects, visual/hearing/skin problems, epilepsy.
Cornelia de Lange syndrome is associated with hypertrichosis and severe **LD**, and its features do **NOT** include large hands and feet — small hands/feet are the characteristic finding.

blocks.text: Cornelia de Lange syndrome features **SMALL** (not large) hands and feet — a 'which is **NOT** a feature' stem uses 'large hands and feet' as the trap answer, playing on the syndrome's other exaggerated features (hypertrichosis, long philtrum).

blocks.text: Foetal alcohol spectrum disorder (**FASD**): no proven safe alcohol level in pregnancy; teratogenic in all three trimesters. **UK** estimate ~1/100 children affected (~6,000-7,000 babies/year). Typically mild **LD** plus speech/language problems; microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, flat philtrum, thin upper lip, short stature. Neurocognitive deficits: impulsivity, hyperactivity, concrete thinking, visuospatial problems, poor judgement/impulse control, memory deficits.
Microcephaly is a characteristic feature of foetal alcohol syndrome (among the listed options, distinguishing it from Fragile X, Down's syndrome, tuberous sclerosis, or hydrocephalus).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Learning Disability_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Congenital hypothyroidism: incidence ~1/4,000, more common in girls; usually mild deficiency with few symptoms. Untreated features: puffy face, large protruding tongue, dry hair, constipation, low muscle tone, jaundice, and cognitive-development failure leading to **LD**.

Homocystinuria (autosomal recessive) mimics Marfan syndrome but with **TIGHT** rather than loose joints: marfanoid stature, chest deformity, dislocated lens, mild **LD** — the key differential in an **EMI** list against Sanfilippo disease (dwarfism, claw hand, joint stiffness, hepatosplenomegaly, severe **LD**).

blocks.text: Homocystinuria mimics Marfan syndrome (marfanoid habitus, lens dislocation) but has **TIGHT** joints versus Marfan's loose joints, and causes only mild **LD** — distinguishing it from Sanfilippo disease (severe **LD**, claw hand, hepatosplenomegaly, dwarfism) in the same **EMI** list tests attention to joint laxity and **LD** severity as the differentiators.

Sanfilippo disease (heparan sulphate breakdown disorder): severe LD, claw hand, hepatosplenomegaly, joint stiffness — a **prominent sleep disorder** is a distinguishing behavioural feature; death typically age 10-20.
Lesch-Nyhan (X-linked recessive, **HGPRT** deficiency): compulsive self-mutilation (biting lips/tongue/fingers, onset 2-3y), choreoathetoid movements, death usually from renal failure.

bullets.text: Hurler syndrome (alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency → glycosaminoglycan accumulation): short stature, hepatosplenomegaly, coarse facial features (hirsutism, corneal clouding, large tongue); developmental arrest by age 2-4 then progressive mental/physical decline; associated hearing loss; death often before age 10.

Laurence-Moon-Biedl syndrome (multiple loci: 11q13, 11q21, 15q22, 3p13): retinitis pigmentosa, polydactyly, spastic paraplegia, night blindness (red cone atrophy), hypogonadism, **NIDDM**, renal problems, central obesity; mild-moderate LD.

Congenital hypothyroidism (incidence ~1/4,000, more common in girls; usually mild): untreated features include puffy face, large protruding tongue, dry hair, constipation, low muscle tone, jaundice, and cognitive-development failure leading to LD.

blocks.text: **LD** occurs in ≥30-==40%== of people with epilepsy; epilepsy prevalence in the **LD** population is ~20-==25%== overall — higher in severe **LD** (30-==50%==) than mild **LD** (15-==20%==).
The prevalence of epilepsy among patients with **LD** is approximately 20-==25%==.

blocks.text: Epilepsy can be misdiagnosed in **LD**, particularly where there is sudden unexplained aggression, self-mutilation, or bizarre behaviour, including abnormal/stereotyped movements, fixed staring, rapid eye-blinking, exaggerated startle, attention deficits, or unexplained intermittent lethargy. Behavioural problems may also arise from antiepileptic drugs (e.g. phenobarbitone, primidone, benzodiazepines, **vigabatrin**), especially with brain injury/**LD**. Up to ==70%== of people with **LD** achieve good seizure control without major side effects.

Epilepsy prevalence by syndrome: Down's syndrome 5-==10%==, Fragile X 20-==25%== (usually mild, easily controlled, often resolving in adolescence — resembling benign Rolandic epilepsy), Angelman syndrome >==90%==, Rett syndrome ==90%==, tuberous sclerosis ==90%== (often presenting as infantile spasms). Epilepsy is also common (up to ==100%==) in the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses and other metabolic causes of **LD** (sialidosis type 1, Tay-Sachs disease, type 3 Gaucher disease, mitochondrial encephalopathy with lactic acidosis and strokes, myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres).

blocks.text: Infantile spasms/West syndrome (triad: infantile spasms + hypsarrhythmia + **LD**): onset usually 4-6 months, ==90%== within the first year; Moro-like flexion spasms of neck/trunk/arms/legs, often symmetric with an associated cry; **EEG** shows chaotic high-voltage slow waves with diffuse/asynchronous spikes (hypsarrhythmia).

Lennox-Gastaut syndrome: **LD** with multiple generalised seizure types (tonic, clonic, atonic, absence); **EEG** often shows multiple spikes; prognosis is often poor. Onset usually before age 8 (peak 3-5y); cognitive impairment **WORSENS** over time — a progressive **INCREASE** in **IQ** is **NOT** a feature (the opposite is true: most patients develop serious intellectual problems within 5 years of onset).
Lennox-Gastaut syndrome does **NOT** feature a progressive increase in **IQ** — cognitive impairment deteriorates, not improves, with disease course.
